Tutorial note 
Statement 2 is incorrect because personal pension contributions do not affect taxable income. 
Instead basic rate tax relief is given at source and higher rate relief is given by extending the 
basic and higher rate bands by the amount of the gross contribution of £8,600 (£6,880 × 
100/80).  
Statement 3 is incorrect because HM Revenue & Customs would have contributed £1,720 i.e. 
the basic rate tax deducted at source (£6,880 × 20/80). 
Statement 1 is correct because the basic rate band for 2025/26 is extended by the gross 
amount of the personal pension contributions (£6,880 × 100/80= £8,600). This reduces the 
income falling in the higher rate band by £8,600. 
Statement 4 is correct as Charles’ adjusted net income would have been £8,600 lower as a 
result of deducting the gross personal pension contribution of £8,600. This would increase the 
personal allowance by £8,600 × 50% = £4,300 as the ANI in excess of £100,000 has decreased.

Examiner’s report 
The income tax question involved Jason. He was employed by Initial plc as a sales manager, 
but was considering resigning on 14 March 2025 and taking up an offer of employment with 
Subsequent plc which would commence on 15 March 2025. If employed by Subsequent plc, 
Jason would receive a higher base salary and more benefits compared to remaining 
employed by Initial plc. However, Jason wanted to know how much more income tax he 
would have to pay should he take up the new offer of employment. 
Part (a) for 2 marks required candidates to state one advantage and one disadvantage for an 
employee if their employer payrolled the taxabl e benefits provided to the employee. This 
section was not particularly well answered. 
Rather than just being asked to explain payro lling of benefits, candidates are also expected 
to know the advantages and disadvantages if an employer payrolls the taxable benefits 
provided to an employee. For example, an advantage to the employee could be either: 
• There is no need to declare payrolled benefits on the employee’s self-assessment tax 
return, or 
• The employee will not have any unexpected tax liabilities in respect of the taxable 
benefits which have been payrolled. 
And a disadvantage would be: 
• The tax due on the benefit will generally be  paid earlier than if collected under self-
assessment. 
Part (b) for 11 marks required a calculation of how much more income tax Jason would have 
had to pay for the tax year 2025/26 if he took up the offer of employment with Subsequent 
plc rather than remaining employed by Initial plc. This section was reasonably well answered. 
• Candidates should simply list any exempt items within the main computation and 
indicate as such by the use of zero (0) – not by an explanation. 
• Even though there might only be a ½ mark fo r recognising an exemption, it is important 
to know the various exemptions so that time is not spent in producing more 
complicated workings. 
• Candidates should note that many of the workings for this style of question can be 
included within the main computation. For example, the beneficial loan working 
(£140,000 × 3.75% × 8/12 = £3,500). The only aspect which warranted a separate 
working here was the living accommodation additional benefit. 
• With computations containing both additions and deductions, candidates should be 
very careful to indicate which is which. A single column approach with deductions 
included as such on the spreadsheet avoids any confusion. 
• Jason was clearly an additional rate taxpayer under both employment alternatives, so 
the extra amount of income tax payable was simply the difference between the two 
amounts of employment income multiplied by the rate of 45%. Producing two income 
tax workings not only used more time, but meant that a mistake was much more likely. 
Practice as many computations as possible. If this is done, straightforward workings for the 
main benefits should become second nature, meaning that marks can be obtained quite 
quickly without making any basic mistakes.

Examiner’s report 
The income tax question was based around Poppy who was employed by Zune plc and was 
also a member of a partnership.  
Zune plc provided Poppy with a diesel car (not meeting the real driving emissions 2 (RDE2) 
standard) and two mobile telephones. These benefits were all payrolled.  
Poppy had been in partnership with Rose and Teasel, but Teasel resigned as a partner on 6 July 
2025; the partners always sharing profits and losses equally. For the year ended 5 April 2026, 
the partnership had a tax adjusted trading loss (before taking account of capital allowances). 
The partnership’s only asset was a car used by Poppy which was sold on 31 July 2025.  
Poppy’s only other income was the accrued in terest from gilts which were purchased on 
1 August 2025 and sold on 31 October 2025. 
The three requirements were all fairly straightforward, so it was surprising that this question 
was not better answered. 
Requirement (a) – 10 marks 
Although the employment aspects of this requirement were well answered by most 
candidates, a number of candidates struggled to correctly allocate the trading loss. The 
interaction of capital allowances and loss relief was a particular issue. The calculation of the

The 10-mark higher skills question involved Kazou. He was employed at a gross annual salary 
of £200,000 (so an additional rate taxpayer) but  planned to retire on 5 April 2029. At that 
point, Kazou’s income will reduce to gross a nnual pension income of £55,000 (so a higher 
rate taxpayer). 
Kazuo was going to undertake £40,000 of work on a freelance basis during the year ended 
5 April 2026, and will do this via a new limited company, Zaoku Ltd. 
Kazuo was looking at three alternative ways of extracting the profits of Zaoku Ltd: 
Alternative 1: After allowing for corporation tax, Kazuo will withdraw the entire net of tax 
profits as dividends during the tax year 2025/26. 
Alternative 2: Kazuo will be paid gross directors' remuneration of £8,000 and Zaoku Ltd will 
make a pension contribution of £32,000 into a company occupational pension scheme on 
Kazuo's behalf during the tax year 2025/26. 
Alternative 3:  The net of tax profits will be left undrawn in Zaoku Ltd until the tax year 
2029/30 when Kazuo has retired. He will then withdraw the entire net of tax amount as 
dividends in the tax year 2029/30. 
Although there were a number of perfect answers, many candidates found this question 
quite challenging. One particular problem was that candidates did not appreciate that part 
(c) was essentially the same as part (a), but set a few years ahead with a lower tax rate. This 
future setting confused a significant minority of candidates, with a number calculating 
income and taxes over several years. However, the question clearly stated that the freelance 
work would only last for just one year, from 6 April 2025 to 5 April 2026. 
Requirement (a) – 3 marks 
This requirement was generally fairly well answered, and there were many perfect answers. 
Although candidates had the option of using a full calculation approach, working at the 
margin was easier and quicker. There was also less scope for making arithmetical errors. 
Unless opting for a full computation approach, the only relevance of Kazuo’s salary of 
£200,000 was to establish the rate of tax applicable (and it was stated that Kazuo was an 
additional rate taxpayer in any case). However, a number of candidates included this amount 
within their corporation tax computation, and this then had a knock-on effect throughout 
the remainder of the answer. 
If using a working at the margin approach for the income tax calculation, this was simply (for 
two marks): 
£40,000 (freelance earnings) – £7,600 (corporation tax as calculated) – £500 (dividend nil rate 
band) multiplied by the dividend additional tax rate of 39.35% 
Common problems included using the gross earnings (rather than the net of tax figure) and 
using an incorrect rate of tax. Given the rates of tax are provided, it made no sense to lose a 
half-mark by carelessly using, for example, 39.55% instead of 39.35%.

Examiner’s report 
The income tax question was based around Sheldon who was employed by Luqe Ltd. 
This question was very well answered, with a number of perfect responses. However, quite 
a few candidates failed to achieve fairly easy marks due to poor examination technique 
and/or not reading the question carefully enough. 
Although there were various ways of approaching this question, the easiest one was to have 
a main computation with workings for employment income and for property income. Of 
course, many candidates had a lot more workings than this, which would have taken more 
time and made it more difficult to keep track of all the relevant figures. 
As regards poor examination technique, one of the main problems here was not showing 
workings. If workings are shown, marks will still be given even if an arithmetical mistake is 
made. For example, one candidate incorrectly showed the beneficial loan as ((£80,000 –
£72,000)/2) × 3.75% × 8/12 = £100. The correct calculation was ((£80,000 + £72,000)/2) × 
3.75% × 8/12 = £1,900. However, because they had shown their workings, they were awarded 
1 of the available 1.5 marks. 
As regards not reading the question carefu lly enough, there were two quite common 
mistakes made that were costly in terms of marks: 
• Luqe Ltd provided Sheldon with living accommodation. Even though the question 
stated that living accommodation was provided throughout the tax year, a number of 
candidates misread the subsequent statement that Sheldon first moved into the 
property on 1 January 2025. They took this to be the 1 January during the tax year in 
question (which would have been 1 January 2026) and then restricted living 
accommodation benefits by 3/12ths. 
• For the property income expenses, it was stated that Sheldon’s expenditure was 
£35,800 for the tax year. This figure included three amounts, only one of which was 
disallowable (£1,600 for legal fees in relation to the grant of a five-year lease). The 
deduction was therefore a quite straightforward £35,800 – £1,600 = £34,200. 
However, many candidates either ignored the total figure of £35,800, deducted 
£35,800 along with some or all the other fi gures, or deducted an adjusted version of 
£35,800 along with some or all the other figures. There were two marks for the correct 
deduction, but the incorrect variations scored poorly. 
Candidates should avoid putting detailed workings within the one cell because it is too easy 
to make a mistake with the syntax. Referring to the beneficial loan working again, one 
mistake that cropped up several times was (£80,000 + £72,000/2) = £116,000 rather than the 
correct ((£80,000 + £72,000)/2) = £76,000. Although candidates are not usually penalised for 
such obvious errors, it will be an issue where more complicated workings are involved. 
Candidates who rush their response, can sometime s fail to spot the obvious. Before taking 
account of benefits or other income, Sheldon had a gross annual salary of £126,000. This 
level of income by itself meant that Sheldon was not entitled to any personal allowance and 
was an additional rate taxpayer. The personal allowance was sometimes given regardless, 
and the tax rate applied to Sheldon’s dividend income was sometimes not 39.35%. 
Looking at some of the other half marks on this question: 
•  The half mark for the use of Luqe Ltd’s company gym being an exempt benefit was 
picked up by virtually every candidate.

sum, premium bond prizes and the interest from the ISA) should simply have been listed 
within the main computation and indicated as such by the use of zero (0) – not by an 
explanation.

manner. There was no need to justify the non-availability given the level of Kagan’s

Part (c) for 2 marks required candidates to state for each of the four alternative investments

inheritance tax. Therefore, the replacement of the quoted shares with either premium 
bonds, an ISA or freehold property would not have changed the value of Kagan’s chargeable 
estate. However, the investment in the pension fund (which is not withdrawn) would have 
been outside of Kagan’s estate, thereby reducing his potential IHT liability.

Examiner’s report 
This question involved an individual who was planning to purchase a residential freehold 
property which was going to be let out. She was unsure whether to purchase the property 
personally or via a limited company. The limited company would be incorporated for the sole 
purpose of purchasing and letting out the property, and Kat would hold all of the shares in 
the company. The company’s corporation tax liability was provided in the question. 
Part (a) for 9 marks required candidates to determine if there would be an overall saving of 
tax if Kat purchased the property via a limited company rather than purchasing it personally. 
Those candidates who made sure that they understood the scenario and worked carefully 
through each calculation had no difficulty answering this section. 
As warned in previous reports, where a tax figure is given for one of the scenarios (in this 
case, the corporation tax figure), candidates sh ould never attempt to recalculate the figure 
for themselves. All this does is use up valuable  time. As regards the conclusion, this should 
have just been a calculation of the tax difference between the two scenarios. There was no 
need for a detailed explanation. 
Where computations are required for two different scenarios, candidates should clearly 
indicate which scenario is being answered. This is particularly important where some of the 
same information is used in both scenarios. In this case employment income and the personal 
allowance were common across both scenarios. Some candidates attempted to answer this 
question with just the one computation; impossible given that property income formed part 
of the first computation, with dividend income included in the second. 
It should have been quite clear from the info rmation provided that full computations were 
necessary for both scenarios. Those candidates who calculated the tax liability for a personal 
purchase and then attempted to adjust the figures for a corporate purchase invariably ended 
up with a very confused answer. 
The personal purchase required candidates to apply the restriction whereby relief for 100% 
of property income finance costs is restricted to the basic rate.  
Working through past examination questions will help candidates familiarise themselves with 
the best approach to be taken when answering questions which examine more than one tax. 
Also, it is important that candidates appreciate the interactions that can arise in such 
questions, and an article has been published covering many of the scenarios which could be 
examined. 
Part (b) for 1 mark required an explanation of one way in which the calculation of a future 
taxable gain on a property disposal made by the limited company would differ from the 
calculation of a taxable gain on a disposal made personally by Kat. Although there were many 
good answers to this section, some candidate s discussed the finance costs restriction when 
this has nothing to do with taxable gains. All that was required was a brief mention (not a 
detailed answer) of the annual exempt amount.

Although a higher skills question, candidates were instructed to produce full income tax and 
NIC computations. Candidates seem to prefer this approach (compared to working at the 
margin), and this largely explains the very good performance. 
There were many perfect answers to both aspects of requirement (a). 
Existing arrangements 
In regard to the existing arrangements, a number of candidates did not appreciate that the 
allowance received by Bertie for business mile age in his private car was tax-free with no 
expense claim possible. This was because the a llowance of 45 pence per mile is exactly the 
amount of authorised mileage allowance permitted by HM Revenue & Customs. 
When it came to the income tax computation, a fairly common mistake was to not appreciate 
that Bertie’s liability was solely at 20% given the extent that the basic rate band was extended 
by his personal pension contributions. 
With the calculation of employee class 1 NIC, quite a few candidates did not use Bertie’s gross 
director’s remuneration of £75,000 as the limiting figure. Instead, the taxable income figure 
was often used, or a figure adjusted for personal pension contributions and/or the mileage 
allowance. 
Beneficial arrangements 
In regard to the beneficial arrangements, there were various mistakes: 
•  Normal tax rates were sometimes applied instead of the dividend tax rates; 
•  It was not appreciated that with just dividend income, there would be no NIC payable; 
•  The car benefit – although correctly calculated – was sometimes shown as separate to 
the main income tax calculation (the basic rate of 20% was then applied, even though 
the benefit was clearly covered by Bertie’s personal allowance); and 
•  Rebite Ltd’s pension contributions on Bertie’s behalf were taken into account despite 
being an exempt benefit. 
Again, there were many perfect answers to requirement (b). 
One particular problem was that a number of candidates recalculated Rebite Ltd’s 
corporation tax liability under the existing arrangements, despite being instructed not to do 
so – this figure was being provided. If the correct figure was recalculated, this was just a case 
of some time being wasted. However, an incorrect calculation meant both wasted time and 
the inability to get the half-mark. This is why it is so important to read through the question 
carefully, especially the requirements along with any guidance notes.  
The computation itself was fairly straightforward, and half the marks would have been given 
if just the trading profit of £340,000 was taxed at 25%, with this figure then compared to the 
given corporation tax liability under the existing arrangements. To get full marks, it was also 
necessary to deduct the leasing costs and the pension contributions.  
The dividends paid to Bertie were irrelevant, although some candidates insisted on deducting 
them. This is why question practice is so important because this is the type of mistake which 
when made once, candidates learn not to repeat.

partners continued to trade as a partnership. They were also provided with the total amount 
of class 1 employee and employer NICs in respect of the director’s remuneration to be paid 
by Triple A Ltd. A number of candidates, however, wasted time by calculating NIC figures. 
Overall, this question was reasonably well answered. Those candidates who tried to use the 
provided partners’ income tax figure as a ba sis for calculating the income tax payable by 
directors, invariably did not achieve a pass mark. 
A surprising number of candidates had difficulty, despite a very similar example being 
available in the higher skills article. It is im portant to appreciate the interactions that can 
arise in a higher skills question, and reading published articles and practising exam standard 
questions will help to this end.  
Requirement (i) 
This was a very straightforward computation provided candidates ignored the pension 
contributions made by Triple A Ltd, and used the correct rate of tax for the dividend income. 
There was a mark for knowing that the pension contributions were exempt, but this was only 
given if this point was indicated by either a zero entry or an explanation. Many candidates 
did not do this, thereby missing the very easy mark.

Because all three directors had the same income, the correct approach was to do the one 
income tax calculation and to then multiply the end result by three. Quite a number of 
candidates wasted time (even if it was just a matter of copy and paste) by producing three 
separate, but exactly the same, computations. 
Requirement (ii) 
The corporation tax working for Triple A Ltd was somewhat more difficult, although there 
were a number of perfect answers.  
Candidates had to start with the company’s taxable total profits (figure provided), then 
deduct the total director’s remuneration, class 1 employer NICs and pension scheme 
contributions (all these figures were provided). It was necessary, however, to multiply the 
provided figures for director’s remuneration and pension scheme contributions by three – 
the number of directors.  
Dividends should be ignored, although quite a few candidates deducted them.  
Another mistake sometimes made was to deduct the class 1 employee NICs as well as, or 
instead of, the employer NICs. If this was done, the half mark for correctly deducting just the 
employer NICs was not given.  
Provided the correct figures were deducted, candidates would then have had a revised 
taxable total profits figure of below £50,000. The corporation tax calculation was therefore 
at the single rate of 19%.  
If any of the figures were missed, candidates would have been faced with a more difficult 
marginal relief calculation for equivalent marks. With no dividend income, this could have of 
course been calculated as £50,000 at 19%, with the balance of profits charged at 26.5%. 
Requirement (iii) 
The comparison meant pulling to gether figures from both the scenario as well as ones 
calculated.  
The comparison was between the total tax and NIC liabilities for the partners if they had 
continued to trade as a partnership (these figures were all provided) and the total income 
tax liabilities of the directors (calculated), the corporation tax liability of Triple A Ltd 
(calculated) and the class 1 employee and employer NICs (figures provided).  
Most candidates achieved at least some marks here, with many gaining the full 1.5 marks. 
The most common mistake was to omit the corporation tax payable by Triple A Ltd.

text:
March 2019 OT question 
Hana was UK resident in the tax year 2024/25. He worked full time in Egypt in the tax year 
2025/26. 
What is the maximum number of days which Hana can spend in the UK and be treated as 
automatically not resident in the UK for the tax year 2025/26?
working:
4 C 
Examiner’s report 
This question examines the third automatic non-UK residency test. For an individual to meet 
this test, and therefore be treated as automatically not resident in the UK for the tax year 
2025/26, they would have to work full-time overseas and spend less than 91 days in the UK. 
Therefore, because Hana worked full-time in Egypt throughout 2025/26, he will be treated 
as automatically not resident in the UK for the tax year as long as he spends no more than 90 
days in the UK. 
The correct answer is therefore C, however, answer option A was most commonly chosen. 
This would be the correct answer using the sufficient ties tests. However, the sufficient ties 
tests are only used to determine residence status if none of the automatic non-UK residence 
tests (and none of the automatic UK residence tests) is met. 
This suggests that candidates may not have be en familiar enough with the residence tests 
and the procedure to determine residence.

Statement B is incorrect. It is not possible for Zara to claim the transferable personal

personal allowance neither spouse/civil partner can be a higher or additional rate taxpayer.

be taxed at the higher rate of 40%, than under the current 50:50 split.

Examiner’s report 
This question examines knowledge of the deadlin e for an individual taxpayer to claim relief 
for a trading loss which they wish to offset in the tax year prior to the tax year in which the 
loss arose. The correct answer is option B (31 January 2028), as a claim must be made within 
one year of 31 January following the end of the tax year in which the loss arose. Therefore, 
as the loss arose in the tax year 2025/26, a claim for relief must be made by 31 January 2028. 
Option B was the most common answer selected but a significant number of candidates also 
chose each of the other answer options, suggesting that many candidates were not well 
prepared for a question on this topic. The second most common answer was option A 
(31 January 2027) which is the deadline for submitting a personal tax return online for the 
tax year 2025/26. Candidates may have selected  this date as they are familiar with this 
deadline in relation to the tax year 2025/26 and assumed the deadline for claiming the loss 
would be the same. 
Administration deadlines, both for individuals and companies, are an important part of the 
syllabus and future candidates are reminded of the importance of learning, and being able 
to distinguish between, the different deadlines as part of their studies.

Anika sold her entire holding of 3,000 £1 ordinary shares in Distribo Ltd, a trading company, 
to her son, Hemi, for £53,000 on 14 July 2025. The market value of the shares on that date 
was £98,000. Anika had purchased the 3,000 shares on 28 October 2012 for £41,500. She has

What is the amount of gift (holdover) relief (if any) which could be claimed in respect of 
the disposal of these shares?
working:
156 C 
 £ 
Proceeds (MV) 98,000 
Less: Cost (41,500) 
 ––––––– 
Gain before relief 56,500 
Gift holdover relief (balancing figure) (45,000) 
 ––––––– 
Chargeable gain (£53,000 – £41,500) 11,500 
 ––––––– 
 
 
Tutorial note 
The full gain cannot be deferred using gift holdover relief where there are actual proceeds in 
excess of cost (i.e. the donor has made a profit). In this case the actual proceeds of £53,000 
exceeded the cost by £11,500. Therefore £11,500 of the gain is chargeable immediately and 
only the balance can be deferred using gift holdover relief. 
There is no requirement for the donor to work at the company or to have held the shares for 
a minimum time period when claiming gift holdover relief in relation to shares. These are 
requirements for BADR.

Heng is a wealthy 45 year old who would like to reduce the potential inheritance tax liability 
on her estate when she dies.

Making lifetime gifts to trusts up to the value of the nil rate band every seven years

Changing the terms of her w ill so that the residue of her estate goes to her husband

Making lifetime gifts to her grandchildren early in life

Tutorial note 
Option A describes the common inheritance tax planning technique of ‘skipping a generation’. 
This technique can maximise the inheritance available to future generations as a charge to 
inheritance tax will only arise once, on th e passing of the estate residue to Heng’s 
grandchildren. If the residue had been left to Heng’s children and they subsequently gifted 
the assets to their children, two charges to inheritance tax would arise.  
That being said, skipping a generation woul d not reduce Heng’s potential inheritance tax 
liability on death as legacies left to both children and grandchildren are equally chargeable.

Examiner’s report 
This question tested candidates’ knowledge of the payment of IHT on a chargeable lifetime 
transfer (CLT) to a trust. The donor, Sandeep, is primarily liable for the tax due on a CLT and 
the due date is the later of the following: 
(i) Six months after the end of the month of transfer 
(ii) 30 April after the end of the tax year of transfer 
The later of these dates is therefore 31 May 2026 and so the correct answer was D. Many 
candidates were able to select the correct date, but were less successful in determining who 
was primarily liable for payment. Tax administration and the payment of tax are important 
aspects of the syllabus and candidates are reminded to devote sufficient attention to these 
topics when preparing for the TX UK exam.

As is typical for the 10-mark question, different taxes were covered, in this case namely

outstanding interest-only mortgages, and Aurora’s main residence.  
• As regards capital gains tax, it was the chargeable gains, periods of ownership and the 
periods which Aurora had lived in each property.

Aurora and her deceased husba nd, Andrew, having made lifetime gifts which fully utilised 
their respective inheritance tax nil rate bands of £325,000. This being the case, the nil rate 
bands could simply be ignored. Only the residence nil rate bands were relevant.

deducting the annual exempt amount. Therefor e, the annual exempt amount and the tax 
liability were irrelevant, and could not possibly gain any marks.

Examiner’s report 
This question was on inheritance tax (IHT), and candidates found this to be a challenging area.  
The requirement for part (a) was to calculate the IHT payable as a result of a taxpayer’s death, 
and to state who was responsible for paying the tax. The taxpayer had made (1) a chargeable 
lifetime transfer (more than seven years before death), (2) a potentially exempt transfer and 
(3) another chargeable lifetime transfer. A quick review of the information given should have 
indicated that no lifetime tax would have been paid (this fact was actually stated in respect 
of the second chargeable lifetime transfer) and that taper relief was not relevant (given that 
none of the gifts were between four and seven years of death). However, many candidates 
dedicated a lot of time to establishing this. Candidates should read through the question 
carefully before they begin their calculations.  
Part (b) required an explanation as to why it might have been beneficial if the taxpayer had 
left a portion of their estate to his nephew rather than to his brother. This aspect was well 
answered, with most candidates appreciating the basic IHT planning of avoiding a double 
charge to tax.  
The IHT planning in part (c) was less well understood. It was necessary to explain why it might 
be advantageous to make lifetime gifts even when such gifts are made within seven years of 
death. The main advantage here is that the value of the gift is fixed at the time it is made, so 
no IHT is payable on the increase in value between making the gift and the time of death. 
Taper relief may also be available.

Examiner’s report 
The 10-mark higher skills question involved Jess ica, an additional rate taxpayer. On 6 April 
2025, she had made a lifetime gift consisting of  both shares and cash to a trust, with the 
funds then being held for the benefit of her two grandchildren aged three and four. 
Although this question was well answered, the fact that the same share information had to 
be used for both capital gains tax and inheritance tax purposes often caused confusion. This 
is despite a similar example being included in the higher skills, chargeable gains and 
inheritance tax articles. It is important to appreciate the interactions that can arise in a higher 
skills question, and reading publis hed articles and practising exam standard questions will 
help to this end. 
Requirement (a) 
The relevant information to pull out from the question is that Jessica made a gift of 100,000 
£1 ordinary shares in Valuable Ltd to the trust. With Valuable Ltd having a share capital of 
250,000 £1 ordinary shares, the gift represents a 40% shareholding, so the relevant deemed 
proceeds figure is based on £4 per share. The shares were acquired at a £1 par value. 
Therefore, the gain is simply 100,000 × £3 (£4 – £1) = £300,000 (for 2 marks). Deduct the 
annual exempt amount, multiply by the higher capital gains tax rate (since Jessica is an 
additional rate taxpayer), and that gives the capital gains tax figure. 
Provided the valuation basis is understood, that should be a very easy and quick 3 marks. 
The big problem for many candidates, of course, was that they used an inheritance tax basis 
of valuation. A common error was to calculate the inheritance tax value (£900,000 – part (b)) 
and then deduct the correct cost figure of £100,000 (100,000 at £1). This would have wasted 
a minute or two on the erroneous calculation. 
Requirement (b)  
The diminution in value of Jessica’s estate wa s a cash element of £250,000 (for one mark), 
and the 100,000 £1 ordinary shares in Valuab le Ltd. Before the transfer, Jessica owned 
150,000 shares; a 60% shareholding valued at £7 per share. After the transfer, Jessica owned 
50,000 shares; a 20% shareholding valued at £3 per share. The diminution in value from the 
gift of shares was therefore (150,000 at £7) – (50,000 at £3) = £900,000 (for 2 marks). 
 

--- PAGE 522 ---

476  KAPLAN PUBLISHING 
The total value of the transfer was therefore £1,150,000 (£250,000 + £900,000). It was then 
just a case of deducting the full nil rate band of £325,000, with lifetime tax calculated at the 
rate of 20% (since the trust paid the inheritance tax arising). 
This requirement was quite well answered, although a very common mistake was to exclude 
the £50,000 held within cash ISAs from the cash element of £250,000. Even though the 
requirement was to ignore the inheritance tax annual exemption, quite a few candidates still 
deducted this. Despite the scenario clearly stating that the trust paid the inheritance tax 
arising, a number of candidates grossed up the tax due using a rate of 20/80ths. 
Requirement (c) 
The gift impacted on Jessica’s savings income and her dividend income. 
Savings income: If the gift had not been made, Jessica would have received savings income 
of £6,250 on the cash held during the tax year, of which £1,250 would have been from ISAs. 
Dividend income: If the gift had not been made, Jessica would have had dividend income of 
£24,000. This was reduced to £8,000 as a result of making the gift of shares. 
There were many perfect answers to this requirement, although answers were often more 
complicated than they needed to be. 
Savings income: The ISA intere st was not relevant (being exempt), so the income tax 
reduction was simply £5,000 (£6,250 – £1,250) at 45% = £2,250 for 1.5 marks. Any attempt 
to include the personal allowance made it impossible to score full marks. 
Dividend income: Here, the income tax reduction was £16,000 (£24,000 – £8,000) at 39.35% 
= £6,296 for 1.5 marks. The dividend nil rate band often caused unnecessary complications, 
although full marks were still available if the nil rate band was deducted from both ‘before 
gift’ and ‘after gift’ computations. 
Candidates should be careful to use the correct tax rates which are clearly shown in the tax 
tables available in the exam.

Examiner’s report 
An accounting period starts when the company becomes liable to corporation tax, in this case 
the company started to earn interest (on which it will pay corporation tax) on the 1 March 
2025. An accounting period will finish when the company starts to trade and this will start a 
new accounting period. Therefore, the first accounting period will be from 1 March 2025 to 
31 March 2025. A financial year (FY) starts on 1 April and ends on 31 March and is identified 
by the calendar year in which it begins. In this case the accounting period 1 March to 31 March 
2025 falls within the FY2024 (starting on 1 April 2024 and ending on 31 March 2025). 
The accounting period from 1 April 2025 to 31 March 2026 is the second accounting period 
for corporation tax purposes (when trade starts and running to the maximum period of 
12 months) and that falls into FY2025 (starting on 1 April 2025).

Tutorial note 
A large company is required to pay its final instalment of corporation tax by the 14th day of 
the 4th month after the end of the accounting period (AP). Note that for a 12-month AP this 
is 16 months after the start of the AP. 
Where an AP is less than 12 months, the first instalment is due by the 14th day of the 
7th month after the start of the AP. Subsequent instalments are due at 3 monthly intervals 
thereafter, until the date of the final instalment is reached. 
For an eight-month AP instalments are due on the 14th day of months 7, 10 and 12 (the last 
being 4 months after the end of the AP). For this scenario, that is 14  July 2025, 14 October 
2025 and 14 December 2025. 
The first two instalments are calculated as 3/8 × corporation tax liability (£400,000 × 3/8 = 
£150,000). The final instalment will be 2/8 × corporation tax liability.

period. When reading through the question, candidates should therefore take a note that 
this is going to impact on the calculation of the lease premium deduction, capital allowances 
and property business income.  
Then when candidates are planning the layout of their answer, it should be apparent that 
separate workings are only required for the lease premium and capital allowances. 
Everything else can be dealt with within the main computation, with just one column 
required for the figures. Note how the workings for interest payable and for the property 
business income are included in the model answer.

The main computation must commence with the computation of Harbour Ltd’s operating 
profit, which is then followed by other inco me (property business income and chargeable 
gain). The corporation tax figure follows after the main computation.  
There are two very important points here:  
Negative figures should be clearly shown by entering them as such on the spreadsheet. It is 
very difficult for markers to pick up negative figures if all figures are shown positive, with the 
total calculated within the cell on the lines of A1 + A2 – A3 + A4. It is also very easy to make 
mistakes using this approach. If negative figures are entered, the total is simply SUM(A1:A4). 
Requirement (a) – 10 marks 
As the note states, answers should commence with the operating profit. Any different 
approach makes an answer quite difficult to mark, especially an answer which attempts to 
rewrite the statement of profit or loss.  
Figures should not be combined. For example, the amortisation add back of £1,300 and the 
lease premium deduction of £806 should not be shown as £494, especially as £494 was also 
a fairly common incorrect answer for the lease premium deduction. It should also be noted 
that since the lease premium consists of a payment, it simply cannot result in an income 
entry.  
There are a couple of aspects which require obvious care:  
• Interest paid in the statement of profit or loss is £24,600. Accruals at the beginning 
and end of the period are £20,500 and £12, 300 respectively. The correct figure (on a 
payable basis) to deduct in working out the trading profit is therefore £24,600 – 
£20,500 + £12,300 = £16,400.  
• With the property business income, the rent has been received for six months, but the 
insurance paid for 12 months. Given the four-month accounting period, the calculation 
is therefore (£15,600 × 4/6) – (£1,800 × 4/12) = £9,800.  
Question practice will eliminate mistakes such as giving an annual exempt amount (which is 
not available for companies) against the chargeable gain, thereby losing a very easy ½ mark. 
Also, candidates should appreciate that both the annual investment allowance and [first 
year] allowance are given for the same asset if the annual investment allowance expenditure 
limit is exceeded. In this case, the annual investment expenditure limit was reduced to 
£1,000,000 × 4/12 = £333,333 because of the four-month accounting period.  
Requirement (b)(i) – 3 marks 
The fact that this requirement is just for 3 marks, together with the use of ‘briefly’ should be 
a very good indication that only a short set of answers is required. This is why it is important 
to make use of the model answers since candidates’ answers should not be any longer.  
If tax evasion and tax avoidance are muddled up, the available marks are obviously going to 
be lost, so candidates should think first, writ e second. The key point is that tax evasion is 
illegal, whereas tax avoidance is legal. 
As regards Harbour Ltd extending its accounting period, the company can do this provided 
company law requirements are met (and these are not relevant to the tax examination). 
Therefore, candidates cannot expect to get the full mark available if there [are] any caveats 
to their answer. HM Revenue & Customs will not s ee this is as tax evasion, nor is there any 
possibility of a compliance check being carried as a result of the change.

The question was generally very well answered, with many candidates scoring high marks.

into two accounting periods), and a half mark for the period from 1 October 2025 (from the

This requirement was generally well answered, although many candidates either did not 
appreciate that there was an accounting period running from 1 October 2025 to 28 February 
2026, or they had just the one period running from 1 May 2025 to 28 February 2026. 
Requirement (b) – 9 marks 
With this type of answer containing additions and deductions, candidates should be careful 
to indicate which is which. A single column approach with deductions included as such on the 
spreadsheet avoids any confusion. It is then just a matter of using the SUM function to get to 
a figure for taxable total profits. Candidates who added up their total figure on a cell-by-cell 
basis (e.g. A1 + A2 + A3 etc) invariably had problems when it came to negative entries, and it 
was sometimes difficult for markers to determine whether a figure was a plus or a minus.

were simply £220,000 at 100%, and £30,000 at 18% (for one mark in each case), and the gain 
was calculated as the proceeds of £204,000 less the reinvestment of £168,000 (1.5 marks).

caused problems were the two interest figures and the chargeable gain. It was somewhat 
surprising to see a number of candidates adding the figure for interest payable and deducting 
the figure for interest receivable. Such carelessness cost a half mark in each case.  
With the chargeable gain, it was clearly stated that Elara Ltd had made a claim to rollover the 
gain, so this should have represented a fairly easy 1.5 marks.  
Many candidates forgot to make the deduction for the qualifying charitable donations, even 
where they had correctly added them back earlier in their computation. 
Requirement (c) – 4 marks 
There were quite a number of perfect answers to this requirement, although a number of 
candidates did not appreciate that payment of a dividend and the advance rental payment 
would not impact Fenrir Ltd’s corporation tax liability for year ending 31 March 2026. This is 
because dividends are paid out of post-tax profits, and (given the accruals basis of accounts 
preparation) rent paid in advance would not be deductible for the year ended 31 March 2026.  
Having worked out the adjustments, candidates then needed to calculate the tax saving. This 
could either be done by multiplying the adjustment by the corporation tax rate of 25%, or 
working out a revised corporation tax liability and comparing this to the previous liability.  
Well prepared candidates were able to answer this requirement quickly (a benefit of question 
practice), scoring a fairly straightforward four marks and saving time. However, a correct 
answer for the car – along with the 25% tax saving – was sufficient to score half of the marks.

Examiner’s report 
The corporation tax question was generally very well answered, with many candidates 
scoring high marks. 
Requirement (a) – 15 marks 
Commencing with the operating profit, candidates were required to adjust for the following: 
Disallowable expenditure (2.5 marks): There were five items to consider, and these were all 
non-allowable. The majority of candidates correctly adjusted for four or five of the items, 
although the amortisation and/or the qualif ying charitable donations were sometimes 
missed. For this style of question, it is very important that candidates clearly indicate whether 
items are being added or deducted. A single column layout is therefore recommended. 
Leasehold premium (3 marks):  Many candidates had no difficulty calculating the correct 
deduction for the grant of a 12-year lease. One common mistake, however, was to work out 
the non-chargeable portion of the lease (£96,000 × 2% × (12 – 1) = £21,120) and then use 
that for the basis of the lease deduction rather than working out the chargeable portion 
(£96,000 – £21,120 = £74,880). Although most candidates appreciated that the chargeable 
portion then had to be divided by the number of years of the lease (12 years), quite a few did 
not then apply the 6/12ths restriction; the lease being granted on 1 October 2025. 
An alternative approach to calculating the chargeable portion of the lease was £96,000 × (51 
– 12)/50 = £74,880. If using this approach, candidates needed to take care as the incorrect 
number of years (51 years and 12 years) were often used. 
It was also important to realise that the final result had to be deducted in the main 
computation. 
Regardless of approach, it is not recommended to attempt the entire working within the one 
spreadsheet cell. For example, missing the brackets on £96,000 × 51 – 12/50 would give an 
answer of £4,896,000. Provided the correct wo rkings are shown, appropriate marks will be 
awarded even if a candidate makes an arithmetical error. Without workings, it can be difficult 
determining what the candidate’s intention is. 
Capital allowances (5.5 marks):  There were quite a lot of marks for a capital allowances 
computation, so care was needed. It was pleasing to see many perfect answers, but some 
candidates struggled here. It was necessary to decide whether an asset purchase qualified 
for the 100% annual investment allowance, and, if not qualifying , whether the purchase went 
into the main pool or the special rate pool.  
The aspect which caused most difficulty was the disposal of the car purchased during the 
same year. The correct treatment was to add the addition and to deduct the disposal 
proceeds from the special rate pool. However, many candidates kept this car separate and 
calculated a balancing adjustment. 
Other income (2 marks):  The other income consisted of bank interest (it was necessary to 
add in a year end accrual), dividends from an 80% UK subsidiary company (this was exempt 
income) and a chargeable gain (the profit before taking account of the indexation allowance 
was also given). 
Once again, there were a lot of perfect answers here. Typical mistakes included deducting 
the bank interest accrual, treating the dividend as taxable, and using the pre-indexed gain or 
deducting the annual exempt amount of £3,000. This is why question practice is so important 
because these are the type of mistakes which if made once, are less likely to be repeated.

Tutor’s top tips 
Being able to determine when corporation tax is payable is a common examination 
requirement, and it is important to learn the rules about which companies must pay by 
quarterly instalments and the exceptions from that system, which are relevant here. 
• Large companies have to make quarterly instalment payments in respect of their 
corporation tax liability. A large comp any is one with augmented profits 
exceeding £1,500,000, adjusted for sh ort accounting periods and associated 
companies. 
• However, a company is not required to make quarterly instalment payments in 
the first year that it is large.  
Therefore, E-Commerce plc will not have been required to make instalment 
payments for the year ended 31 March 2026 as it was not a large company in 
the year ended 31 March 2025.  
This is because the augmented profits of £1,360,000 were less than £1,500,000. 
• For the year ended 31 March 2027, this exception will not apply. Therefore, 
E-Commerce plc will have to make quarterly instalment payments as its 
augmented profits will exceed £1,500,000.

Examiner’s report 
The corporation tax question was very well answered, with many candidates scoring high 
marks. The question required candidates to calculate Cop Ltd’s trading loss and taxable total 
profits for the three-month period 1 October to 31 December. 
As for the income tax question, there were various ways of approaching this question. Again, 
the easiest one was to have a main computation working out the trading loss, with this then 
extended to include the chargeable gain and qualifying charitable donation to arrive at a 
figure for taxable total profits. Capital allowances and the chargeable gain both warranted 
separate workings. 
In regard to the main computation, there were two issues which sometimes caused 
problems: 
• Candidates were instructed to indicate by the use of zero (0) any items which did not 
require adjustment. There were in fact five items of expenditure where no adjustment
 was required (because they were allowable), representing a total of 2.5 marks. A 
number of candidates did not do as instructed and therefore would not have gained 
these very easy 2.5 marks even if the remainder of their workings were correct. 
Remember it is important to read and follow the instructions given in the requirement. 
• With this type of answer containing both additions and deductions, candidates should 
be very careful to indicate which is which. A single column approach with deductions 
shown clearly as such on the spreadsheet avoids any confusion. Those candidates who 
did not show the deductions clearly invariably had problems when it came to showing 
totals with negative entries, and it was sometimes difficult for markers to determine 
whether a figure was a plus or a minus. 
One other point to bear in mind is that candidates should answer a question in the order in 
which information is provided. The information was provided in the order (1) donations, (2) 
legal and professional fees, (3) promotional costs and (4) annual party. So, adjustments 
should follow the same sequence. If this a pproach is followed, it allows markers the 
opportunity to sometimes award a mark where an obvious mistake has been made. 
Capital allowances 
The fact that the accounting period was only three months long meant care had to be taken 
with the capital allowances working: 
• The £1,000,000 annual investment allowance expenditure limit was £1,000,000 × 3/12 
= £250,000. 
• There was no restriction in regard to first-year allowances. 
• The 18% and 6% writing down allowances were both restricted by 3/12ths. 
Despite these complications, quite a number of candidates correctly calculated the capital 
allowances figure for 5 marks, with many achieving 4 or 4.5 marks. 
The main problem was with the car in the specia l rate pool which was bought (for £57,000) 
and sold (for £50,000) during the accounting period. Despite this being the only asset in the 
special rate pool, there was not a balancing adjustment, but, instead, a writing down 
allowance calculated as normal.

(a) Capital gains group 
• Companies form a capital gains group if at  each level in the group structure there 
is a 75% shareholding, provided the parent company has an effective interest of 
more than 50%.  
• Alto Ltd, Bass Ltd, Cello Ltd, Echo Inc and Flute Ltd are all 75% subsidiaries, and 
Music plc has an effective interest of 60% (80% × 75%) in Flute Ltd. All of these 
companies therefore form a capital gains group. 
• However, Bass Ltd and Cello Ltd will only be included in respect of assets 
acquired or disposed of whilst they were members of the group. 
• Drum Ltd and Gong Ltd are not included as Drum Ltd is not a 75% subsidiary, 
and Music plc’s effective interest in Gong Ltd is only 48% (80% × 75% × 80%). 
• Although Echo Inc is included in the definition of the capital gains group, 
companies that are resident overseas are not able to take advantage of the 
provisions applicable to a capital gains group. 
(b) Associated companies 
• Alto Ltd, Bass Ltd, Cello Ltd, Echo In c, Flute Ltd and Gong Ltd are all under the 
common control of Music plc, and are therefore associated companies. 
• Companies associated for part of the accounting period, such as Bass Ltd and 
Cello Ltd, count as associated companies for the whole of the period. 
• For these purposes, it does not matter where a company is resident. Echo Inc is 
therefore included despite being resident overseas. 
• Drum Ltd is not included as an associated company since Music plc’s effective 
interest in this company is only 45%.
